items.title: L7: Choosing between two vacancies and planning the work
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; GOV.UK, Civil Service Success Profiles
items.body: When two vacancies appeal, compare them on facts rather than on a first impression. Start with the closing dates and the stage dates, because an interview date can clash with a test date or with a holiday. Check how each role is assessed: a role that sifts on one lead behaviour and a short statement takes far less preparation than one asking for several behaviours, a strengths interview and a test. Compare the grade, the location and working pattern, the contract type and the clearance level. Then compare the evidence: which role lets you use examples you already have? You can often reuse the same strong example for two applications if the behaviours overlap, but each answer must be rewritten to fit the wording and word limit. Plan backwards from each deadline. Write the longest answers first, leave a day for a trusted person to read them, and submit with time to spare. Do not apply for both roles just to increase your odds if you cannot give each a proper effort; two rushed applications usually score lower than one careful one. It is however sensible to apply for two roles you can do properly, because campaigns are competitive and one outcome does not decide the other. Record the reference numbers, the dates and the stage reached in a simple tracker.

questions.prompt: Two roles close on the same Friday. One needs a 250-word statement; the other needs three 250-word behaviours and a test. Rhea has six free evenings. What is the best plan?

options.text: Apply to the shorter one only, since two applications always lower both scores
Leave both until Thursday so the examples are fresh in her mind
Start the longer application first and finish it early, then use the remaining time on the statement
Spend five evenings on the statement because it is shorter to read, then rush the heavier one on the last night

questions.hint: Plan the heavier workload first and leave time to review both before submitting.

questions.prompt: Both of Omar's applications ask about Delivering at Pace. How should he use his one strong example?

options.text: Use it in both but drop the Result in one, to avoid obvious repetition
Rewrite it for each advert, fitting each question's wording and word limit
Use it in one application and make up a second example for the other
Paste the same text into both, because consistency helps the markers compare them

questions.hint: Reuse the experience, but write each answer to the specific question.

questions.prompt: Which comparison of two adverts is the most useful to a candidate with a week to spare?

options.text: Which stages each has and whether the dates clash with her commitments
Which advert was published first, since earlier adverts tend to be less competitive
Which advert has the more senior-sounding job title, as it will pay better
Which advert is longer, since length shows how serious the department is

questions.hint: Stages and dates are practical factors that decide whether you can do the application well.

questions.prompt: An interview date for one role clashes with a test date for another Kofi wants. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Plan to attend both by leaving the first session early
Pick the role with the higher salary and withdraw from the other
Wait until the day and see which one feels easier to attend
Ask a named contact if another slot is possible

questions.hint: Asking early may resolve the clash; departments often have some flexibility.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to apply to a large number of roles with minimal effort on each?

options.text: Civil Service Jobs blocks accounts that apply to too many roles in a month
Departments allow only two live applications per candidate at any time
Each new application lowers the score of the one before it
Rushed applications tend to score lower than a few careful ones

questions.hint: Quality of evidence drives scores more than the number of applications.

questions.prompt: Which entry in a tracker is most useful?

options.text: A copy of the department's logo and the job summary
Reference, closing date, stage and next date
Only the job title and the advertised salary
The names of the other people who have applied

questions.hint: A tracker should help you act on dates and recall what you submitted.

questions.prompt: Lena's two vacancies close in six days and ten days. What is the best order of work?

options.text: Finish the earlier one first, noting examples the second can reuse
Ignore the second until the first has been decided, so she can learn from the result
Do the later one first, since it has more time and needs more thought
Submit both on the earlier closing date, to be safe

questions.hint: Meet the earlier deadline first but begin thinking about the second.

questions.prompt: One advert needs Security Check clearance; the other needs none beyond baseline checks. What does this change for planning?

options.text: The second will skip the pre-employment checks
The first will be assessed more strictly at the sift, because the role is sensitive
The first needs extra time after the offer for vetting
The first requires candidates to pay for their own vetting

questions.hint: Higher clearance usually means a longer pre-employment process.

questions.prompt: Which factor should not be the main reason for choosing a role?

options.text: A belief that a senior title is easier to sift
Whether the location and working pattern suit you
Whether you can show the essential criteria with examples
Whether the stage dates fit your commitments

questions.hint: Seniority does not make a sift easier; criteria and fit matter.

questions.prompt: Reggie is offered an interview for Role A. Role B, which he prefers, has not yet reached its sift. What is sensible?

options.text: Withdraw from Role A to keep his options clear for Role B
Postpone Role A's interview for as long as the department allows
Accept anything Role A offers, then drop out of Role B without a word
Attend Role A and ask Role B's contact about timings

questions.hint: A genuine opportunity should be pursued while being honest about timelines.

items.title: L7: Making limited experience count
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles; GOV.UK, Civil Service Behaviours
items.body: Entry-level roles do not assume a long work history. Markers want evidence of the behaviour, not a particular job title. Useful sources include part-time or temporary work, voluntary work, study, caring responsibilities, community or sports roles, and running a household budget. The key test is whether you did something specific, with a result. A well-chosen small example beats a vague large one. Take Communicating and Influencing. A student who explained a changed timetable to anxious classmates, using a short email and a drop-in session, shows communication adapted to an audience, whereas 'I have good communication skills' shows nothing. For Managing a Quality Service, a volunteer who checked every parcel list against stock sheets and cut missing items shows attention to quality. Be wary of exaggeration: if you were part of a group, say what your part was. Do not claim a management title that you did not hold. If you have gaps in your history, give a short honest explanation in the application where there is space, and be ready to describe the period at interview. Experience for essential criteria must be real and verifiable at checks. Where the advert asks for a qualification, such as English and maths at a given level, you must hold it, and informal skills cannot replace it.

questions.prompt: A candidate has never had a paid job. Which evidence would a marker accept for Changing and Improving?

options.text: A statement that they have always been open to new ideas
A list of personal qualities taken from an online quiz
Trying a new booking sheet at a youth club, with fewer clashes
The title 'Youth Leader', with a list of the clubs they have attended

questions.hint: Specific actions and results count wherever they happened.

questions.prompt: Which is the weakest evidence of Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: 'I briefed new starters on the rota and asked them to repeat it back to check.'
'I have excellent communication skills and I get on with everybody.'
'I rewrote the volunteer instructions in plain English and the confusion stopped.'
'I explained the change to a worried customer and agreed a follow-up call.'

questions.hint: A general claim without an event shows nothing.

questions.prompt: Jas was one of six people who organised a charity event. What should her answer say?

options.text: That the event raised money, leaving her own role unstated
What she did herself, such as booking the venue, and the result
That she led the group, since the marker needs to see leadership
That the whole group organised it, which is fair to the other five

questions.hint: Markers score the individual's behaviour, so describe your own part honestly.

questions.prompt: The advert lists a specific qualification as essential and a candidate lacks it. What is the best view?

options.text: The department will waive it for candidates who offer to study for it later
The panel will decide on the day whether it matters
It will not replace it, so check whether an equivalent is accepted
A very strong statement will make up for it, as the sift looks at the whole picture

questions.hint: Essential qualifications must be held; check equivalents with the contact.

questions.prompt: Which statement would a careful candidate avoid?

options.text: 'I managed a team of five', when they only covered shifts
'I supported a manager by checking the weekly figures'
'I covered shifts and helped train a new colleague'
'I was part of a team, and my own tasks were the rota and the stock count'

questions.hint: Over-claiming can be exposed at interview or in checks.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate treat a gap in the employment history?

options.text: Leave it unexplained, since panels never ask about gaps
Give a long explanation covering every detail of that period
Stretch the dates of the neighbouring jobs so the gap disappears
Give a brief honest explanation and be ready to discuss it

questions.hint: Honesty with brevity is best; checks may test dates.

questions.prompt: Which example best shows Managing a Quality Service from a caring role?

options.text: Explaining how rewarding it is to care for a relative day after day
Giving the number of hours she spends caring for her relative each week
Keeping a medication record for a relative and fixing a gap in it
Saying that caring has made her patient, calm and good in a crisis

questions.hint: Quality is shown by checking, spotting problems and acting.

questions.prompt: What makes a small, specific example better than a vague large one?

options.text: It is more likely to be true, because small things are easier to recall
It lets the candidate leave out the STAR structure entirely
It takes fewer words, which markers say they prefer to read
It names an action and a result a marker can score

questions.hint: Specific actions and results are what get credited.

questions.prompt: Which activity could provide evidence for Making Effective Decisions?

options.text: Choosing the cheapest option each time without comparing alternatives
Choosing between two suppliers using prices and reviews
Waiting for someone else to choose and then agreeing with them
Following a supervisor's instructions exactly, without question

questions.hint: The behaviour involves weighing evidence and justifying a decision.

questions.prompt: A candidate's best example is eight years old. How will it be treated?

options.text: It can be used if still the best, though recent evidence weighs more
It will be accepted only if it was gained in the Civil Service
It will be accepted only if it was paid work
It will be rejected, because the sift accepts nothing older than two years

questions.hint: Age of evidence is not a bar, but recent evidence tends to carry more weight.

items.title: L7: Strengths-based questions and quick answers
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles, strengths guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: Strengths-based questions look at what energises you and what you do well, rather than asking for a past example. Success Profiles describe strengths as the things a person does regularly, does well and enjoys. Panels may ask short questions, such as 'What are you really good at?', 'What kind of task do you put off?' or 'Do you prefer to plan or to improvise?'. Because answers are short, panels look at energy, tone and detail. They often score on how quickly and naturally you respond, how specific your example is, and whether it shows enthusiasm for the kind of work that the job involves. Preparation cannot be scripted in the way a behaviour answer can, though you can reflect on your genuine preferences and on tasks you lose track of time doing. A strengths interview is often paired with behaviour questions. Do not invent a strength you do not have: the role may involve many tasks you are asked to do in practice, and a mismatch will show at work as well as interview. If a question asks about a weakness or something you dislike, answer honestly and show what you do about it, rather than naming a trivial or disguised strength. If you are asked about a task you find draining, avoid describing a core part of the job as something you hate. It is fine to take a moment to think before answering.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical feature of a strengths-based question?

options.text: It always requires a past example in full STAR form
It asks you to recite policy from memory
It asks for a written case study before the interview
It asks what you enjoy and do naturally

questions.hint: Strengths questions test natural preference and energy.

questions.prompt: A panel asks Imran, 'Which tasks do you put off?'. His role is mainly data checking. What is the best answer?

options.text: An honest answer on a task he avoids and how he copes
'Checking data, because it is dull, though I do it anyway'
'None; I enjoy every task equally'
A long story about a time he missed a deadline

questions.hint: Honesty plus management of the weakness is better than a dodge or naming the core work.

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate avoid inventing a strength?

options.text: Strengths are not scored, so there is no need
A mismatch shows later in the job
Panels dislike enthusiastic candidates
A genuine strength is always on the CV already

questions.hint: Genuine strengths are easier to describe and fit the role better.

questions.prompt: How does preparing for a strengths interview differ from preparing for behaviour questions?

options.text: You prepare nothing at all, because strengths cannot be assessed
You rehearse only the dates and times of the interview
You reflect on genuine preferences, not scripted examples
You memorise answers word for word, as the questions are fixed

questions.hint: Strengths are about what you naturally enjoy, so rehearse thinking rather than text.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign of a strong strengths answer?

options.text: A long list of positive qualities
A short refusal to answer
A specific task example and why it energises you
A statement of what the employer must provide for you

questions.hint: Specific detail and energy make an answer credible.

questions.prompt: Success Profiles describe a strength as something a person...

options.text: does only when closely supervised
has been told is important by their manager
has a certificate to prove
does regularly, does well and enjoys

questions.hint: Strengths are repeated, well done and energising.

questions.prompt: A panel member asks a question and Dee needs a moment to think. What is the best approach?

options.text: Pause briefly and then answer clearly
Ask to skip the question and return to it later
Fill the silence with loosely related detail while she thinks
Say the first thing that comes to mind, whatever its fit

questions.hint: A short pause is fine; rambling is not.

questions.prompt: Which pair of questions is most likely to appear in the same interview?

options.text: A written policy essay and a speech
A strengths and a behaviour question
A medical examination and a language test
A coding task and a driving test

questions.hint: Success Profiles often combine strengths and behaviours.

questions.prompt: What do panels look for in a strengths answer?

options.text: Whether the candidate agrees with the panel
Energy, specific detail and fit with the work
Whether the answer repeats the question word for word
Whether it lasts longer than a minute

questions.hint: Panels look for evidence of natural fit, not length.

questions.prompt: Which response to 'What are you not so good at?' best shows self-awareness?

options.text: 'I have not thought about it, so I would rather not answer that one'
'I do not really have any weaknesses that affect my work at all'
'I can get caught in detail, so I set time limits and check priorities'
'I work too hard and care too much about getting the result right'

questions.hint: A genuine weakness with a practical response is credible.

items.title: L7: Declaring interests and keeping the panel fair
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: A fair panel is one whose members have no interest that could affect their judgement. Under the Recruitment Principles and the Civil Service Code, a panel member who knows a candidate personally, or is related to them, or has a close working relationship, must declare it before shortlisting. The usual outcome is that the member steps down from that campaign or from assessing that candidate, and the declaration and decision are recorded. A relationship does not have to be a family one: a close friendship, a business interest or a recent line-management link may also need to be declared. Candidates also have duties. If a candidate knows a panel member, they should mention it when applying or as soon as they learn who is on the panel, so the department can manage it. Candidates should not contact panel members to seek an advantage or to discuss their application outside the official process. Panels are usually made up of more than one person, trained in the process, and often include someone from outside the immediate team to provide challenge. Scores should be based on evidence recorded against the criteria, and notes should be kept in case of a query. Where a panel member is also a hiring manager, they should still score using the same criteria as the others and be moderated.

questions.prompt: Sana learns that one interviewer is her former line manager from three years ago. What should she do?

options.text: Tell the contact so the panel can be reviewed
Contact the manager privately to ask for a fair hearing
Say nothing, since a former manager is not a family member
Withdraw her application, since it can never be fair now

questions.hint: Declaring a relationship lets the department manage the risk properly.

questions.prompt: A panel member realises when the shortlist is circulated that a candidate is a close friend. What should the panel member do?

options.text: Ask the friend to withdraw quietly
Mark the friend as normal without telling anyone
Mark the friend more strictly to avoid any favouritism
Declare it and stand aside from that candidate

questions.hint: Declaration and a recorded decision protect the process.

questions.prompt: Which relationship may need to be declared by a panel member?

options.text: A close friendship or recent management link
Having shared a train carriage with them once
Having the same surname as a candidate by coincidence
Having read the candidate's name in a staff newsletter

questions.hint: The test is whether the relationship could reasonably affect judgement.

questions.prompt: Why are panels usually made up of more than one person?

options.text: It spreads the cost of the interview between teams
It makes interviews longer, which gives candidates more time
Several assessors give challenge and reduce bias
It allows the hiring manager to be outvoted every time

questions.hint: Multiple assessors help consistent, fair scoring.

questions.prompt: Which action by a candidate is inappropriate?

options.text: Requesting feedback after the outcome
Privately lobbying a panel member
Asking the named contact a question about the role
Telling the department they know a panel member

questions.hint: Private lobbying undermines fair and open competition.

questions.prompt: What should panel scoring be based on?

options.text: How well the panel got on with each candidate
A general impression formed over the whole day
Which candidate would be easiest to manage
Evidence recorded against set criteria

questions.hint: Evidence-based scoring supports fairness and defensibility.

questions.prompt: Why are notes kept after an interview?

options.text: They let scores be explained if a candidate asks or complains
They are reused to write the next advert
They are destroyed straight away to protect candidates' privacy
They are sent to every candidate automatically

questions.hint: Records show how a decision was reached.

questions.prompt: The hiring manager sits on the panel. What is correct?

options.text: They give the final mark after the others have left
They may overrule the other panel members if they disagree
They score only the internal candidates
Same criteria as the others, with moderated marks

questions.hint: The hiring manager must follow the same process.

questions.prompt: Hamid learns that a candidate for his team is his cousin. What is the proper response?

options.text: Assess the cousin last so the panel can compare the others first
Declare it and take no part in assessing that candidate
Ask the other panel members to ignore the connection
Assess the cousin normally, since the scoring is evidence based

questions.hint: Family relationships must be declared and managed.

questions.prompt: What is the likely result if a conflict of interest is declared early?

options.text: The conflict is ignored if the panel member is senior
The campaign is cancelled automatically and re-advertised
It can be managed, such as by changing the panel
The candidate concerned is excluded from the competition

questions.hint: Early declaration keeps the process safe.

items.title: L7: When adjustments are disputed or complicated
items.source: Equality Act 2010; EHRC, Employment statutory code of practice
items.body: The duty to make reasonable adjustments in recruitment is about removing disadvantage, and what is reasonable depends on the circumstances. Relevant factors include how effective the change would be, how practical it is, its cost and the organisation's resources, and the disruption it would cause. A very large organisation such as a government department is expected to meet a high standard. Candidates are not always required to name a diagnosis; they should explain what difficulty they face and what would help. Departments may ask for more detail where needed to understand the barrier, and should treat what they learn as confidential. If a request is refused or only partly met, a candidate can ask for the reason, offer an alternative that would work, and raise a complaint through the department's process. It is often helpful to put the request in writing. Adjustments should not change what is being tested. For example, extra time in a reading test is acceptable, but removing the reading element from a role that depends on reading would change the standard. An adjustment can be a different method of assessment, such as an oral answer in place of a written one, if the competence tested remains the same. A department must not make an adjustment dependent on a candidate being cheaper or easier to deal with than others.

questions.prompt: Which is a relevant factor when deciding whether an adjustment is reasonable?

options.text: Whether the candidate has applied to the department before
How popular the candidate is with the panel
Effectiveness, practicality, cost and resources
Whether the other candidates agree to it

questions.hint: These are the usual factors in deciding reasonableness.

questions.prompt: A candidate asks for a screen-reader-compatible test and the department says it is inconvenient. What should the candidate do?

options.text: Take the standard test without comment
Accept the refusal, since inconvenience is enough to justify it
Withdraw and make no complaint, to avoid a dispute
Ask for the reason, suggest an alternative, then complain

questions.hint: Inconvenience alone is rarely a good reason for a large organisation to refuse.

questions.prompt: Which change would alter the standard being tested?

options.text: Giving extra time for a reading test
Dropping the core reading task of the role
Allowing a different font and colour for the text
Providing breaks during a long test

questions.hint: An adjustment should not remove the core competence tested.

questions.prompt: Must a candidate always give a full diagnosis to get an adjustment?

options.text: Not necessarily; explain the difficulty and what would help
Only to the interview panel, who will then decide if the need is genuine
Always, in full medical detail, so that the need can be proved to the panel
Never; the department must make adjustments without asking any questions

questions.hint: Departments need enough information to understand the barrier.

questions.prompt: Why is it helpful to put an adjustment request in writing?

options.text: It speeds up the sift
It gives a clear record of what was agreed
It guarantees the request will be accepted
It removes the department's duty to respond

questions.hint: A written record helps if there is a later dispute.

questions.prompt: Which is an acceptable alternative way of assessing a candidate?

options.text: Giving the candidate a higher score to compensate
Replacing the criterion with an easier one
An oral answer in place of a written one
Skipping the criterion altogether

questions.hint: Alternative methods are fine if the same competence is assessed.

questions.prompt: A department says it will make an adjustment only if the candidate is otherwise 'low maintenance'. Why is this wrong?

options.text: It must not depend on convenience to the employer
Every candidate must be given exactly the same adjustments
Departments cannot refuse any request
Adjustments only apply after appointment

questions.hint: The duty is not conditional on convenience.

questions.prompt: A large government department says it lacks resources for an adjustment. How is this treated?

options.text: It always justifies a refusal, whatever the size of the organisation
It is irrelevant, because cost can never be taken into account
It applies only to small teams, and large departments must always agree
Large organisations face a high standard, so it is weighed but rarely decisive

questions.hint: Resources are considered, and size sets higher expectations.

questions.prompt: Who should know the details of a candidate's adjustment request?

options.text: Only those who need to know in order to arrange it
The other candidates, so the process is transparent
The candidate's current employer
All members of the department

questions.hint: Information must be handled confidentially.

questions.prompt: Priya's agreed adjustments were not provided on the day. What is the sensible step afterwards?

options.text: Say nothing, assuming it made no difference
Write at once, say what happened, ask for a remedy
Wait to see whether she is rejected before saying anything
Post about the panel on social media

questions.hint: Prompt written notice gives the department a chance to correct and is useful evidence.

items.title: L7: When offers are delayed or the facts do not match
items.source: Cabinet Office, Baseline Personnel Security Standard; GOV.UK
items.body: After a conditional offer, delays and discrepancies can happen. A common cause is a reference that has not arrived, a document that needs replacing, or an employer who is slow to confirm dates. The candidate can help by chasing their own referees and by supplying documents promptly. If checks reveal that something in the application does not match records, the department will normally give the candidate a chance to explain. A small error, such as a wrong month, is treated differently from a deliberate false statement about a qualification or a conviction. Where there is a genuine mistake, say so quickly and give the correct information. Do not wait to be caught. A department may withdraw an offer if it concludes that an applicant was dishonest, or if a check cannot be completed satisfactorily, and the Civil Service Code requires honesty from everyone who works for it. If an offer is delayed for a long time, a candidate can ask the contact for an update and an estimate of timing, but should avoid resigning until the offer is unconditional. Candidates sometimes receive a start date that is later than first suggested because of vetting. In that case, a candidate with a current job should check the notice arrangements before any commitment, and keep the department informed if circumstances change.

questions.prompt: Elif's reference from a former employer has not arrived after three weeks. What should she do?

options.text: Ask the department to proceed without any reference
Resign from her current job to show commitment
Chase her referee, tell the department, and offer an alternative
Wait without contact, since references are the department's job to obtain

questions.hint: Candidates can help by chasing referees and keeping the department informed.

questions.prompt: Checks show that Marcus gave the wrong month for starting a past job. How is this likely to be treated?

options.text: As proof of lying, leading to automatic withdrawal of the offer
As unimportant, so it is never raised with him
As a reason to reduce his interview score
As a possible genuine mistake, if he corrects it and explains

questions.hint: Small errors are treated differently from deliberate falsehoods.

questions.prompt: Which discrepancy is the most serious?

options.text: A typing slip in the date of birth that he spotted himself
A false claim to hold a degree he does not have
A reference that arrives late
A mistake in a postcode

questions.hint: Deliberate false statements about qualifications go to honesty.

questions.prompt: Why should a candidate correct a mistake as soon as they notice it?

options.text: It is the only way to raise the interview score
The department cannot otherwise find mistakes
It avoids the need for checks
Honesty is expected, and it shows good faith

questions.hint: Early correction is consistent with the Civil Service Code.

questions.prompt: An offer has been delayed for two months without news. What should Nina do?

options.text: Ask for an update and timing, and hold off resigning until it is unconditional
Resign now, since a long delay suggests the offer is certain to be made
Treat the offer as lapsed and stop replying to the department's emails
Withdraw the application and reapply to the same role once it is re-advertised

questions.hint: Seek information, but protect your current position.

questions.prompt: Vetting pushes a start date later than first suggested. Joe has a three-month notice period. What is sensible?

options.text: Ask the department to pay his employer to release him
Ignore his notice and start as soon as vetting allows
Check his notice terms before committing to a date
Resign immediately and negotiate afterwards

questions.hint: Start dates and notice need to fit together.

questions.prompt: Which statement about withdrawing an offer is correct?

options.text: It can be withdrawn only after the candidate has started work
It can be withdrawn only if the candidate asks for it to be withdrawn
It may be withdrawn if checks cannot be satisfactorily completed or dishonesty is found
It cannot be withdrawn once it has been made in writing and accepted

questions.hint: Offers are conditional on satisfactory checks.

questions.prompt: Amara's copy of her passport page was unclear. What is she most likely to be asked to do?

options.text: Accept that the check has failed
A clearer copy or the original
Wait for the department to guess the details
Send a photograph of someone else's page

questions.hint: Documents used in checks must be legible.

questions.prompt: A candidate cannot complete an employment history because an old employer has closed. What might help?

options.text: Payslips or tax records, if accepted
Saying the employer never existed
Leaving that employer out of the history
Naming a made-up contact so the form looks complete

questions.hint: Departments may accept alternative evidence if explained.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to disclose a problem before the checks find it?

options.text: It stops the checks being carried out
It is required by law in every case
It guarantees that the offer stays in place
It shows honesty and allows fair handling

questions.hint: Early disclosure is part of being open.

items.title: L7: Security clearance levels and what they involve
items.source: Cabinet Office, National Security Vetting guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: Different roles need different levels of security checking. The Baseline Personnel Security Standard is the minimum for most posts. Beyond it, National Security Vetting has several levels. Counter-Terrorist Check is for roles with access to certain sensitive sites or information. Security Check is for roles with regular access to secret assets. Developed Vetting is the most detailed, used for the most sensitive roles, and involves a long interview and wider enquiries. The level required is stated in the advert. Higher levels take longer, and the time is not in the candidate's control. Vetting looks at things such as residence history, financial position, criminal record and associations. It does not demand a perfect record; it looks at honesty, reliability and any vulnerability to pressure. Candidates are asked to complete a detailed form, and the department sponsors the application. People who have lived overseas, held other nationalities or had financial difficulties may still be cleared, but should be open about it. Hiding facts is more damaging than the facts themselves. Some roles can start work pending clearance, with limits on access; others cannot start until it is granted. The advert or offer letter usually says which applies. Clearance belongs to a role and a sponsor, and may need to be transferred or reviewed if the person changes jobs.

questions.prompt: Which level of national security vetting is the most detailed?

options.text: The Baseline Personnel Security Standard
Developed Vetting
Counter-Terrorist Check
Security Check

questions.hint: DV is for the most sensitive roles and includes an interview.

questions.prompt: Why do higher levels of vetting take longer?

options.text: Candidates are always slow to complete the forms
Departments process them only once a month
Each one needs a court order
Wider enquiries take more time

questions.hint: More enquiries mean longer timescales.

questions.prompt: Which statement about vetting is correct?

options.text: It disqualifies anyone who has lived abroad for more than a short period
It is identical for every role, whatever the sensitivity of the work
It looks at honesty, reliability and vulnerability to pressure
It demands a spotless financial and personal record before clearance is granted

questions.hint: Vetting assesses risk, not perfection.

questions.prompt: Chloe had a debt problem in the past and fears vetting. What is the best approach?

options.text: Be open about it and explain how it was resolved
Ask a friend to complete the form for her
Leave it off the form, since it is in the past
Withdraw from the process before the form is sent

questions.hint: Concealment is more damaging than the original facts.

questions.prompt: Where does a candidate find which clearance a role needs?

options.text: In the advert, and often again in the offer letter
At the first day of work
In a published national list of roles
From the interview panel chair only, at the interview

questions.hint: The required level is stated in the advert.

questions.prompt: Which statement about starting work before clearance is true?

options.text: Starting before clearance is prohibited for all roles
A start is allowed only for those who hold a lower clearance already
Some roles allow it with limited access; others do not
Every role allows a full start once the form has been submitted

questions.hint: The advert or offer letter says which applies.

questions.prompt: A candidate has held two nationalities. How will this be treated in vetting?

options.text: It is always a bar to clearance
It should be left off the form
It need not be declared, as it is not relevant
Case by case, and it should be declared

questions.hint: Many people with dual nationality are cleared.

questions.prompt: Who sponsors a candidate's clearance application?

options.text: The candidate
The employing department or team
A private company chosen by the candidate
The candidate's referee

questions.hint: Clearance is applied for through the department as sponsor.

questions.prompt: What happens to clearance when a person changes jobs?

options.text: It always transfers without any checking
It may need transferring or reviewing
It becomes permanent
It is cancelled automatically

questions.hint: Clearance is linked to a role and sponsor.

questions.prompt: What is the best advice for someone nervous about a long vetting form?

options.text: Leave out anything that happened a long time ago
Guess dates when unsure rather than ask
Keep answers short to save time
Answer accurately and fully, and ask if unsure

questions.hint: Accurate, complete forms avoid delay and damage.

items.title: L7: Level transfers, loans, secondments and details
items.source: Civil Service HR guidance; Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles
items.body: Existing civil servants have several ways to move that do not involve a normal promotion. A level transfer moves a person to a different post at the same grade, often to another team or department. Many are advertised on Civil Service Jobs and involve a short assessment; some departments ask for a full competition, while others use a simpler approach. A loan or secondment is a temporary move, often for a fixed period, and the person normally keeps their substantive post to return to. A detail is a short-term move within a department to cover a need. These moves usually do not raise pay, but a temporary promotion into a higher post can, and it is treated differently from a permanent promotion. Moves can help build breadth, such as policy, operational delivery or analysis experience, and show evidence for later promotion. They need agreement between the individual, the home line manager and the receiving team, and release dates are usually negotiated. Employment terms can change when the home department and host organisation differ. A person on loan generally stays employed by the lending organisation. Before accepting, ask about pay and allowances, line management, how performance will be assessed, what happens at the end of the period, and whether the time will count towards experience for promotion.

questions.prompt: Which statement defines a level transfer?

options.text: A temporary promotion into a post that is vacant for a few months
A move to another employer under a shared-services agreement
A move to a different post at the same grade
A permanent promotion into the next grade up after a competition

questions.hint: Level transfers keep the grade and change the role or location.

questions.prompt: Which is typical of a loan or secondment?

options.text: It runs for a fixed period, then the person returns
It ends employment with the home department, which pays a settlement
It is permanent, and the home post is closed once the move starts
It changes the person's grade for good, if the host team is happy

questions.hint: Loans and secondments are time-limited.

questions.prompt: Why might a civil servant take a secondment?

options.text: It lets the person skip probation in their next role
It builds breadth that supports later applications
It lets the person avoid being assessed for a year
It gives automatic promotion when the person returns

questions.hint: Breadth and new skills help later career steps.

questions.prompt: Which question should Kiran ask before accepting a loan?

options.text: Who else was offered a loan, and how long they have served
How many people the host team has turned down so far this year
Whether I can choose my own grade when I return to my home team
What pay applies, who manages me, and what happens at the end

questions.hint: Terms and reporting lines matter before agreeing.

questions.prompt: Whose agreement is usually needed for a loan?

options.text: The individual, the home line manager and the receiving team
The Civil Service Commission, which approves every loan in advance
The individual alone, as it is their career
The receiving team alone, because they carry the cost

questions.hint: Release must be agreed by both sides.

questions.prompt: What is a detail, as a type of internal move?

options.text: A disciplinary measure applied after a formal warning
A type of reserve list kept for a single campaign
A short-term move within a department to cover a particular need
A permanent reduction in grade agreed after a performance review

questions.hint: A detail is a short temporary assignment.

questions.prompt: How does a temporary promotion differ from a level transfer?

options.text: Working at a higher grade for a limited period, often at higher pay
It reduces the grade for a limited period while the person trains
It is the same as a level transfer, because both are temporary arrangements
It ends the old contract and starts a new one at the same grade

questions.hint: Temporary promotion is an upward, time-limited step.

questions.prompt: Who usually remains the employer of a person on loan?

options.text: The Civil Service Commission, which holds all loan contracts
The host organisation, once the person has been in place a month
A third-party company that handles the paperwork
The lending organisation

questions.hint: On loan, the home employer generally stays the employer.

questions.prompt: Zoe has done a 12-month secondment. Which is most useful in her next promotion application?

options.text: A description of the host organisation and its role
What she achieved against the behaviours
The fact that a secondment took place, listed in her CV
Her secondment end date and the name of her host manager

questions.hint: Evidence of behaviour and results is what is scored.

questions.prompt: Why do some departments run a fuller competition for a level transfer?

options.text: To avoid advertising the post outside the department
To raise the pay offered for the post
To keep it fair where several people want the post
To delay the appointment until the next financial year

questions.hint: Competing interest calls for a fair process.

items.title: L7: Temporary promotion and fairness to others
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles; Civil Service Code
items.body: A temporary promotion means doing a higher-graded job for a limited time. It often arises when a post is vacant or the post-holder is away. It can be a valuable step, but it raises fairness questions. Giving a temporary promotion to one person without telling others, or repeatedly extending it, can give that person an advantage in later competitions, because they will have recent experience at the higher grade. Departments are expected to follow their own rules and the principles of merit and fairness. Many allow temporary promotions to be made through a lighter process, but long arrangements, usually those lasting around a year or more, are expected to be competed fairly. Ask what process is used, how long it will last and what happens at the end. A temporary promotion does not give a right to the permanent post: the person normally returns to their substantive grade, and any permanent promotion depends on a fair and open competition. Staff who are asked to act up should be clear about pay, the end date and the duties. Managers should record their reasons and avoid creating a de facto promotion by habit. If you believe that a temporary promotion is being used to bypass a fair process, you can raise it with your line manager or HR, and, if unresolved, use the Civil Service Code's route for raising concerns.

questions.prompt: What is a temporary promotion?

options.text: A permanent move into the next grade after a competition
A reduction in duties while the post-holder is on leave
A transfer to the same grade in another department
Working at a higher grade for a limited period

questions.hint: It is time-limited and upward.

questions.prompt: Why do repeated extensions of a temporary promotion raise fairness concerns?

options.text: The person gains recent higher-grade experience others never had
Extensions always cost more than advertising a permanent post would have
Other staff in the team stop being paid while the arrangement runs
Probation rules no longer apply to the person once the first extension is made

questions.hint: Unfair advantage in later competitions is the concern.

questions.prompt: What normally happens at the end of a temporary promotion?

options.text: The person moves to a lower grade permanently as a result of the arrangement ending
The person returns to their substantive grade unless they win a post fairly
The person stays at the higher grade automatically, because the work has been done well
The person's contract ends and they must reapply to the Civil Service

questions.hint: No automatic right to the permanent post.

questions.prompt: Which action by a manager is poor practice?

options.text: Recording why a person was chosen for the arrangement
Setting a clear end date when the temporary promotion starts
Extending it repeatedly without competition or reasons
Explaining pay and duties before the person agrees

questions.hint: Habit can create a de facto promotion without a fair process.

questions.prompt: Rachel suspects that a temporary promotion is being used to avoid a competition. What is a sensible first step?

options.text: Raise it with her line manager or HR
Resign in protest so that the matter is noticed
Refuse to do any work that depends on the arrangement
Post a complaint on a public forum straight away

questions.hint: Use internal routes first.

questions.prompt: If internal routes fail, what does the Civil Service Code provide?

options.text: Appointing an investigator of her own choice
Raising the concern with the Civil Service Commission
Going directly to the press to force a response
Asking a trade body to decide whether the promotion was valid

questions.hint: The Code gives a route to the Commission.

questions.prompt: When are temporary promotions usually expected to be competed fairly?

options.text: Never, as they are always short-term by definition
Only if the person on the arrangement asks for it
Only if they last a single day
Often when they last around a year or more

questions.hint: Long arrangements are expected to be competed.

questions.prompt: What should an employee ask when offered a temporary promotion?

options.text: Who sits on the Civil Service Commission this year
What scores the other candidates were given
Duration, pay and what happens at the end
How many other people applied for the temporary post

questions.hint: Terms matter before agreeing.

questions.prompt: Does a temporary promotion give a right to the permanent post?

options.text: Permanent posts need a fair and open competition
The line manager can confirm the person in the post in writing
Once six months have been served, the post becomes the person's
A probation period in the higher grade confirms the person

questions.hint: Permanent appointment is on merit.

questions.prompt: Why should managers record their reasons?

options.text: To keep the choice confidential from the rest of the team
To delay the decision until the post is advertised
To justify a higher rate of pay
To show the choice was fair and based on merit

questions.hint: Records support accountability.

items.title: L7: Reserve lists and what to do with several outcomes
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles
items.body: Many campaigns end with a merit list. Candidates who pass the interview are ranked by their overall score, and the highest ranked are offered the posts available. Those who passed but were not offered a post may be placed on a reserve list, for a stated period, often around twelve months. If a post becomes available during that time, the next candidate in rank order is normally offered it. This is a fair way to use a campaign without running another, but it means a candidate on a reserve list may hear nothing for months, or may be contacted at short notice. A reserve list does not guarantee a job. Candidates can usually say whether they wish to stay on the list, and may be asked about their preferred location. If you have a reserve-list position and a new job offer elsewhere, be honest with both departments about the timing. If you decline an offer from the list, you may be removed, but practice varies, so check the wording. It can also be possible to be on reserve lists for several campaigns. When you are offered a post from a list, your original score is used; you are not re-assessed, but pre-employment checks still apply. Keep your contact details current in your account so that offers are not missed.

questions.prompt: What is a reserve list at the end of a campaign?

options.text: A list of managers who have posts they cannot fill
A ranked list of candidates who passed but were not offered a post
A list of candidates who were rejected, kept so they cannot reapply
A list of internal staff who have asked to move teams

questions.hint: Reserve lists hold appointable candidates.

questions.prompt: In what order are reserve-list candidates normally offered posts?

options.text: In the order in which they applied
In alphabetical order of their surnames
In rank order of their scores
In order of age, with the oldest first

questions.hint: Rank order is merit-based.

questions.prompt: Does being on a reserve list guarantee a job?

options.text: It does, at any grade the candidate chooses
It does, within a week of the campaign ending
It does not; it depends on whether posts become available
It does, but only in the department that ran the campaign

questions.hint: No guarantee.

questions.prompt: A candidate on a reserve list gets a different job offer. What is the best step?

options.text: Ignore the department that holds the list until they contact you again
Be honest with both departments and decide before the deadline
Hide the reserve list from the new employer, so as not to weaken the offer
Accept both and see which starts first

questions.hint: Honesty protects your reputation.

questions.prompt: Why keep contact details up to date?

options.text: The details are needed only when a candidate sits online tests
The details are used to adjust a candidate's rank on the list
The list is published and candidates are contacted by the public
Offers from the list may come at short notice and be missed

questions.hint: Missed offers can be lost.

questions.prompt: What may happen if a candidate declines an offer from a reserve list?

options.text: They may be removed from the list
They are banned from the Civil Service for a year
They are promoted to the next candidate's grade
They are fined by the department

questions.hint: Practice varies, so check.

questions.prompt: When offered a post from a reserve list, is the candidate usually re-interviewed?

options.text: Only by a short test at the offer stage
Not usually; the original score is used
Only if the post is at a different location
Always, by a new panel at the same grade

questions.hint: The campaign result stands.

questions.prompt: How long might a reserve list last?

options.text: Ten years, in line with the record retention period
One week, until the next campaign opens
Until the next general election
Often around twelve months

questions.hint: Time periods are stated.

questions.prompt: Can a candidate be on reserve lists for several campaigns?

options.text: Each campaign has its own list, so it is possible
Only one list at a time is allowed per candidate
It is allowed only if the grades differ between the campaigns
It is allowed only if the candidate is already a civil servant

questions.hint: Different campaigns have different lists.

questions.prompt: Why is a reserve list a fair way to use a campaign?

options.text: It removes the need for pre-employment checks
It avoids the need for merit, saving time
It reuses a completed merit assessment
It lets managers choose freely from the list

questions.hint: Offers still follow merit order.

items.title: L7: Making a complaint about recruitment
items.source: Civil Service Commission, Recruitment Principles and complaints guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: If you think a recruitment process breached the Recruitment Principles, there is an order to follow. First, raise it with the department that ran the competition, in writing, within the time limit it sets. Describe what you believe happened, which Principle you think was breached, and what you would like done. The department should investigate and reply. If you remain dissatisfied, you may bring a complaint to the Civil Service Commission, which is independent of departments and regulates compliance with the Recruitment Principles. The Commission can look at whether the Principles were followed and, where it finds a breach, may recommend action, such as a review of the process. It does not re-mark the candidates or decide who should have been appointed. A complaint should be about the process, not about disappointment with a decision made properly. Keep it factual, include dates, copies of emails and names of any people involved, and be clear about the outcome you want. Time limits exist, so act promptly. Complaints are separate from a legal claim under employment or equality law, which has its own rules and time limits; a candidate who believes they were discriminated against may have rights under the Equality Act 2010 and may seek advice from an independent source such as ACAS or the Equality Advisory Support Service.

questions.prompt: To whom should a candidate first raise a recruitment complaint?

options.text: The department that ran the competition
The Prime Minister's office
A trade union, which then takes the case on
The press, to gain attention

questions.hint: Departments must be given the chance to respond.

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Commission do with a complaint?

options.text: It re-marks the application against the criteria
It sets the pay for the post
It appoints a new candidate if the complaint is upheld
It considers whether the Principles were followed

questions.hint: It examines compliance, not scores.

questions.prompt: Which is the best content of a complaint?

options.text: A request that all the other candidates be rejected
Facts, dates, emails and the Principle breached
Opinions about the panel's character and past behaviour
A long account of unrelated grievances going back years

questions.hint: Specific facts are easier to investigate.

questions.prompt: Why should a complaint be made promptly?

options.text: Scores are deleted immediately after the campaign
The panel changes every week
Time limits apply, so delay can lose the right
Complaints expire after a day

questions.hint: Delay can lose the right to complain.

questions.prompt: A candidate believes they were discriminated against. What else might apply?

options.text: Only the right to a reserve list place
Only the department's own pay rules, which apply to internal staff
Rights under the Equality Act 2010, with separate time limits
None, because discrimination is covered only by the Commission's review

questions.hint: Discrimination claims follow a separate legal route.

questions.prompt: What might the Commission do if it finds a breach?

options.text: Recommend action, such as a review of the process
Appoint the complainant to the post
Dismiss the panel members involved
Pay compensation to the complainant automatically

questions.hint: Its powers are recommendations about the process.

questions.prompt: Which complaint is most likely to fall outside the Commission's role?

options.text: A panel member had an undeclared conflict of interest
The post was filled without an advert when the Principles required one
The criteria were changed after the closing date
Simple disagreement with a score from a properly run process

questions.hint: It reviews the process, not individual judgements.

questions.prompt: What should a candidate do if the department does not reply?

options.text: Post about the delay online until the department responds
Chase in writing, keep a record, then consider the Commission
Treat silence as a rejection and take no further step at all
Submit the same complaint again to a different department

questions.hint: Records and chasing help the next step.

questions.prompt: Why include copies of emails?

options.text: They are required in every complaint by law
They give evidence to support the account
They shorten the complaint
They replace the need for dates

questions.hint: Evidence helps.

questions.prompt: Which description of the Commission is correct?

options.text: A recruitment agency that places civil servants
Part of each department, reporting to its permanent secretary
An independent regulator of the Recruitment Principles
A trade union for civil servants

questions.hint: Independence is key.

items.title: L7: Spotting discrimination in recruitment situations
items.source: Equality Act 2010; EHRC, Employment statutory code of practice
items.body: The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination because of nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. In recruitment it covers adverts, application forms, selection and offers. Direct discrimination is treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic, for example rejecting a candidate because of their age. Indirect discrimination is when a rule that applies to everyone puts people sharing a characteristic at a particular disadvantage and cannot be justified as a proportionate way of achieving a legitimate aim. Harassment is unwanted conduct related to a characteristic that creates an offensive environment. Victimisation is treating someone badly because they made or supported a complaint. Employers should not ask about a candidate's health before making an offer, other than for limited purposes such as adjustments or checking ability to take part in the assessment. Questions about plans to have children, marital status or religion at interview are risky and generally inappropriate. A genuine occupational requirement may justify a requirement in rare cases. Candidates who face discriminatory conduct can raise it with the department, use its complaints process, and seek advice about their legal rights, noting that time limits apply.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of direct discrimination?

options.text: Using the same questions for all candidates
Asking all candidates to attend on the same day
Publishing the closing date for applications
Rejecting a candidate because of their age

questions.hint: Direct means less favourable treatment because of a protected characteristic.

questions.prompt: A rule requires every candidate for a desk job to be over six feet tall. Which type of discrimination might this be?

options.text: Indirect, because a neutral rule disadvantages a group
Direct only, because the rule names a characteristic
Victimisation, because the rule penalises complainants
Harassment, because the rule creates a hostile atmosphere

questions.hint: A neutral rule can still disadvantage a group.

questions.prompt: What is meant by victimisation in the Equality Act?

options.text: Treating a candidate unfavourably because of their age or race
Applying a neutral rule that disadvantages one group of candidates
Unwanted conduct that creates an offensive atmosphere at interview
Treating someone badly because they made or supported a complaint

questions.hint: It is a retaliation.

questions.prompt: Which interview question is generally inappropriate?

options.text: 'Are you planning to have children?'
'Why do you want this role?'
'Tell us about a time you solved a problem'
'When could you start?'

questions.hint: Such questions risk discrimination.

questions.prompt: When may an employer ask about health in recruitment?

options.text: Only after the first day at work
Never, for any reason
For limited purposes, such as arranging adjustments
Always, before the first interview, to plan the process

questions.hint: Health questions before an offer are restricted.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a protected characteristic?

options.text: Number of jobs held
Religion or belief
Postcode
Political party membership

questions.hint: The Act lists nine characteristics.

questions.prompt: Aaliyah's interviewer repeatedly jokes about her religion and she feels uncomfortable. What type of conduct may this be?

options.text: Victimisation for having made an earlier complaint
Indirect discrimination caused by a neutral selection rule
Direct discrimination in the scoring of her answers
Harassment related to religion or belief

questions.hint: Unwanted conduct creating an offensive environment.

questions.prompt: What might justify indirect discrimination?

options.text: A proportionate way of achieving a legitimate aim
The hiring manager's personal preference for a particular candidate profile
The cost of changing an established practice, whatever its effect
The fact that the practice has always been used by the department

questions.hint: Justification must be proportionate and legitimate.

questions.prompt: Which step is appropriate for a candidate who experiences discrimination?

options.text: Say nothing, to avoid damaging future chances
Contact the other candidates to ask what they experienced
Raise it, complain, and get independent advice
Wait ten years before taking any step

questions.hint: Time limits apply.

questions.prompt: What does a genuine occupational requirement mean?

options.text: A requirement that suits the existing team
A rare case where a characteristic is essential to the job
A requirement chosen by the manager as the preferred profile
A requirement for the best-looking CV

questions.hint: It is narrow and must be justified.
